items.title: LLM-Mediated Findability of Research Datasets
items.abstract: This study evaluates the LLM-mediated findability of research datasets. The sample uses 100 datasets randomly selected from GESIS. Experiments were run using web-search-based models from OpenAI and Gemini. Six different query strategies combine metadata such as topic, geography, time, title, and abstract-derived natural-language research needs. Results show that query design substantially affects retrieval. One variant uses queries with dataset titles to provide the known-item baseline. In contrast, other metadata were used in generic metadata queries, including topic and geographic coverage, with temporal information to emulate user behavior and information needs. Among realistic discovery strategies, the natural-language approach (V6) performs best, achieving 26.4% Strict Source retrieval with OpenAI and 32.2% with Gemini. The findings highlight the importance of prompt design, metadata quality and specificity, web visibility, and identifier consistency for AI-mediated dataset discovery.

items.title: LLM‐guided semantic‐aware trajectory optimization for UAV path planning using environmental context
items.abstract: Summary Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle path planning in urban environments requires both geometric safety and semantic awareness. Conventional planners based on fixed costs or predefined risk models struggle to reflect mission‐dependent semantic priorities. We present a large language model (LLM)‐guided semantic‐aware planning framework in which the LLM serves as a bounded high‐level decision module. OpenStreetMap data are transformed into class‐wise semantic potential fields, and a route‐relative context and natural‐language mission description are used to infer validated semantic modulation coefficients. A deterministic B‐spline optimizer generates smooth paths by jointly considering multiple factors. Comparisons with existing models demonstrate a competitive tradeoff between path efficiency and semantic safety. Mission‐conditioned experiments reveal that different mission descriptions produce distinct semantic policies and path geometries under identical environmental conditions. Reliability analysis indicates that the deterministic downstream planner maintains stable safety‐related performance under context perturbations and stochastic LLM outputs.

items.title: LocalMind OS: Adaptive Multi-Modal Fusion for Privacy-First Offline Knowledge Workspaces
items.abstract: Modern operating systems and productivity tools generate an immense demand for seamless AI integration, spanning from document summarization to on-screen context analysis. While cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs) offer unprecedented capabilities, they introduce severe data privacy risks, particularly when handling sensitive enterprise or personal data. This paper presents LocalMind OS, a project specific, fully offline framework designed for secure, hardware adaptive AI assistance. The framework represents knowledge through localized Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and combines textual document vectors with real-time visual context captured via a non-destructive background thread. The proposed workflow contains multi-format document ingestion, semantic chunking, FAISS HNSW indexing, LLM token streaming via GGUF quantization, and a hotkey-triggered Vision-Language Assistant. Recent research shows that local-first forecasting and RAG benefit significantly from quantization and concurrent background processing to maintain UI fluidity without cloud reliance. LocalMind OS is designed as an independently im plemented framework rather than a reproduction of existing commercial tools like Microsoft Recall. The final experimental study compares LocalMind OS with traditional cloud baselines using metrics such as latency, retrieval precision, and resource footprint, demonstrating that advanced quantization strategies allow commodity hardware to achieve competitive accuracy with absolute data sovereignty. This paper details the mathematical foundation, architectural design, implementation, and rigorous evaluation of LocalMind OS over a multi-week deployment scenario.

items.title: Machine learning based microstructure classification using SEM images and morphological features
items.abstract: Abstract This study implements an approach based on segmentation-based morphological features derived from scanning electron microscopy images. Microstructures were classified as heterogeneous, homogeneous, and partially heterogeneous using physical features extracted through Otsu-based segmentation and morphological operations. The dataset was expanded to 2000 synthetic images using Poisson-based patch synthesis. The performance of Random Forest, K-nearest neighbors, Support Vector Machine, and Extreme Gradient Boosting algorithms was evaluated comparatively. Results demonstrate that the Random Forest model achieved the highest performance with an accuracy of 87.65 % and a Macro-F1 score of 87.83 %. Confusion matrices reveal that the primary source of error across all models is the transition structures. The findings indicate that features provide a robust and interpretable representation for microstructure characterization. This study shows that machine learning approaches based on physical features can produce reliable and generalizable results in microstructure classification problems, proving effective for explainable artificial intelligence applications in the field of materials science.

items.title: MACHINES MAY DETECT, OFFICERS MUST DECIDE: ALGORITHMIC ASSISTANCE AND THE LIMITS OF DELEGATION IN GST ADMINISTRATION
items.abstract: India's Goods and Services Tax (GST) already runs on algorithms: returns are matched by machine, taxpayers are ranked by risk, and invoices are authenticated through a central portal. Within seven weeks in mid-2026, two High Courts quashed GST proceedings tainted by artificial intelligence (AI), and in doing so raised a question that tax law had not previously needed to answer: who is the decision-maker when a machine has done much of the thinking? This article argues that the answer lies in a familiar principle of administrative law rather than in a new body of 'AI law'. A statutory officer may use an algorithm as evidence or as a drafting aid, but may not allow it to stand in for the application of mind that the statute demands. The article distinguishes predictive analytics from generative drafting tools, shows that the recent decisions address only the second, and warns that a doctrine triggered by visible error will miss competent but unaccountable automation. It proposes an 'algorithm-removal test' and a framework of human-accountable algorithmic taxation to give the principle operational content.

items.title: Make it | ’til you fake it: Shallowfake audio as an emerging operational cyber security threat
items.abstract: The growing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) voice synthesis poses significant cyber security and evidential risks, particularly with the rise of hybrid shallowfake audio. This term refers to recordings that merge authentic speech with synthetically generated voice segments. These hybrid manipulations challenge existing forensic audio authentication practices, which have traditionally focused on distinguishing between entirely authentic and fully fabricated recordings. Recent threat assessments, including 2024 findings from INTERPOL, underscore the growing criminal exploitation of synthetic voice technologies and the lack of consistent frameworks to effectively identify hybrid audio manipulations. This situation raises concerns about the continued reliance on legacy forensic methodologies that predate the widespread use of AI speech synthesis tools. This paper explores the procedural and analytical challenges of detecting shallowfake audio through a controlled experimental investigation that mimics realistic manipulation scenarios. Test audio files comprising mixed authentic and synthetic speech were created using affordable, commercially available production tools and examined using established audio authentication techniques. The results reveal that current forensic approaches may not consistently detect hybrid manipulations, especially when recordings are stream-captured or re-recorded after synthetic voice insertion, heightening the risk of evidential misinterpretation. This research identifies significant gaps in standardised forensic protocols and offers practical recommendations for cybercrime professionals. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.

items.title: Mapping Societal Anxiety from the Industrial Era to the AI Age: A Computational Sentiment Analysis of Victorian Literature and Digital Discourse
items.abstract: The rapid acceleration of artificial intelligence and automated systems in the modern era has reignited widespread debate regarding technological displacement, economic alienation, and human redundancy. This paper presents a comparative computational sentiment analysis bridging nineteenth-century industrial literature with contemporary digital discourse on automation. Using Charles Dickens’ Hard Times (1854) as a thematic anchor for First Industrial Revolution anxieties, we analyze literary text against a curated corpus of modern public discourse surrounding artificial intelligence. Employing Python-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools—specifically the NLTK VADER sentiment analysis engine, alongside Matplotlib and Seaborn for statistical data visualization—this study quantifies polarity, compound sentiment distributions, and semantic shifts across both eras. The findings demonstrate striking structural parallels between Victorian anti-industrial alienation and contemporary AI existential dread, confirming that human resistance to structural automation follows recurring socio-psychological patterns.

items.abstract: MARICYBER-6G: AI-Driven Marine Cybersecurity for 6G-Enabled Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks Exhibited at the Cyber Security Conference of the Irish EU Presidency and Cyber Expo (NCSC Conference) , Convention Centre Dublin, 6–8 October 2026 (Cyber Expo). Project: MARI-CYBERWISE Fellowship: Government of Ireland Postdoctoral Fellowship (GOIPD/2025/1090) Affiliation: Department of Electronic and Computer Engineering, University of Limerick, Ireland This repository contains the editable LaTeX source, compiled poster, research figures, references, and supporting assets for the A0 portrait research poster MARICYBER-6G: AI-Driven Marine Cybersecurity for 6G-Enabled Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks. The poster presents an artificial intelligence-driven cybersecurity framework for 6G-enabled Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks (UWSNs), integrating simulation-driven cyber-threat traffic generation, heterogeneous feature construction, deep learning-based intrusion detection, and adaptive mitigation. It examines Normal, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS), and Spoofing traffic in a three-dimensional underwater network comprising 500 nodes within a 1000×1000×1000 m³ volume. The proposed Residual Temporal Attention Network with Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (ReTAN-BiLSTM) combines multi-scale one-dimensional convolution, residual feature refinement, bidirectional temporal modelling, temporal attention, and raw-feature fusion to classify the three traffic classes. The poster includes the UWSN topology, feature-correlation structure, network performance under different traffic conditions, model architecture, learning dynamics, class-wise training performance, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, convergence plots, confusion matrices, and adaptive mitigation results. ReTAN-BiLSTM achieves reported training and test ROC-AUC values of 0.9911 and 0.9868, respectively. items.title: MCGMark: An Encodable and Robust Online Watermark for Tracing LLM-Generated Malicious Code
items.abstract: With the advent of large language models (LLMs), numerous software service providers are developing LLMs tailored for code generation, such as CodeLlama. However, these models can be exploited by malicious developers to generate malicious code, posing severe threats to the software ecosystem. To address this issue, we first conducted an empirical study and built MCGTest , a dataset of \(406\) prompts designed to elicit malicious code from LLMs. Leveraging this dataset, we propose MCGMark , a watermarking method to trace and attribute LLM-generated malicious code. MCGMark subtly embeds user-specific information into generated code by controlling the token selection process, ensuring the watermark is imperceptible. Additionally, MCGMark dynamically adjusts the token selection range to induce the LLM to favor high-probability tokens, thus ensuring code quality. Furthermore, by leveraging code structure, MCGMark avoids embedding watermarks into regions easily modified by attackers, such as comments and variable names, enhancing robustness against tampering. Experiments on several advanced LLMs show that MCGMark successfully embeds watermarks in approximately \(85\%\) of cases, under the constraint of a \(400\) -token limit. Moreover, it maintains code quality and demonstrates strong resilience against common code modification. This approach offers a practical solution for tracing malicious code and mitigating the misuse of LLMs.

items.title: Measuring Perceived Ease of Artificial Intelligence Utilisation: An Adaptation and Psychometric Validation of a Scale among Preservice Mathematics Teachers in Nigerian Context
items.abstract: Perceived ease of use is a foundational construct in technology-acceptance research, yet instruments developed to measure it in relation to artificial intelligence (AI) remain scarce within African teacher-education contexts. Existing scales are rarely re-examined for the specific referent of AI-assisted mathematics learning. This study adapted a six-item Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) from the literature to an AI-in-mathematics-learning context and examined its psychometric properties among drawn 221 preservice mathematics teachers using a multistage non-probability sampling procedure from three higher institutions in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, Nigeria. Confirmatory factor analysis of the initial six-item one-factor model showed inadequate fit (CFI = .886, TLI = .811). However, the removal of two items with low standardised loadings produced a four-item model with an excellent fit (χ²(2) = 2.770, p = .250, CFI = .991, TLI = .972, RMSEA = .042, SRMR = .026). The retained scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency (ω = .723). Non-parametric comparisons revealed no statistically significant difference in PEOU AI across institutional type (Kruskal–Wallis χ²(2) = 3.637, p = .162) or gender (Mann–Whitney U, z = -.567, p = .571). The findings support a psychometrically sound, unidimensional four-item PEOU-AI scale for use in Nigerian mathematics teacher education and suggest that ease-of-use perceptions of AI tools are broadly comparable across the sampled institutions and gender groups.

items.title: Medical Student Engagement and Intention to Practise Medicine Across Undergraduate Years: A Longitudinal Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Medical students’ declining intention to practise medicine threatens workforce sustainability. Addressing this issue is critical to alleviating workforce shortages and improving healthcare delivery. While previous studies have explored factors influencing students’ career intentions, the specific role of multidimensional student engagement, and whether its associations with intention vary across undergraduate years, has not been systematically examined. Method: We analysed a two-year (2020–2021) longitudinal dataset from the China Medical Student Survey using a cohort-sequential design. Five dimensions of engagement were measured: behavioural classroom, behavioural clinical, emotional, cognitive, and agentic engagement. Multilevel growth models were applied to examine changes in intention to practise medicine and year-specific engagement-intention associations. Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) was employed to evaluate robustness under model uncertainty using Posterior Inclusion Probabilities (PIPs). Results: The findings indicated that intention to practise medicine declined through Year 4, with a slight attenuation of the decline in Year 5. Engagement-intention associations varied across years: behavioural classroom engagement showed its largest association in Year 2; behavioural clinical engagement was significant in Years 4–5; cognitive engagement increased across years; and agentic engagement was stronger in Years 4–5 than in earlier years. Emotional engagement was consistently associated with intention across Years 1–5 and accounted for the largest incremental explanatory power; BMA indicated strong evidence for inclusion of emotional and agentic engagement. Conclusion: Engagement is consistently associated with intention to practise medicine, but the salience of engagement dimensions shifts across undergraduate years. Educational strategies should be year-sensitive and developmentally strategic—supporting emotional and cognitive engagement throughout training and cultivating agentic engagement in early years.

items.title: MediNet: Simplifying Federated and Privacy-Preserving AI Deployment in Healthcare
items.abstract: MOTIVATION: The application of Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning (DL) in healthcare is increasingly feasible in principle, yet remains inaccessible in practice for most clinical institutions. Beyond the well-known challenge of data privacy regulations that prevent centralization of patient records, two further barriers limit adoption. First, deploying a federated learning infrastructure requires substantial technical expertise: configuring distributed training environments, implementing privacy-preserving mechanisms such as Differential Privacy (DP), and managing secure inter-institutional communication demands specialized knowledge that most healthcare organizations do not possess. Second, designing and configuring DL models (selecting architectures, tuning hyperparameters, interpreting results) currently requires machine learning expertise that clinical professionals, including researchers and physicians, typically lack. Existing federated learning frameworks address the infrastructure problem but impose a steep learning curve that effectively excludes non-specialized users. A solution that abstracts this complexity, enabling clinicians and biomedical researchers to design, launch, and monitor federated training processes without programming or machine learning expertise, remains absent from the field. RESULTS: To address existing limitations, we introduce MediNet, a comprehensive server-client Federated learning (FL) platform that allows hospitals and research centers to train Machine Learning (ML) and DL models without moving or exposing sensitive data. It offers an intuitive web-based environment that simplifies FL, enabling users to easily select the model and define training criteria while administrators manage permissions and datasets, ensuring granular and autonomous data control. The system automatically constructs and generates the underlying technical configuration (e.g., Python/FL scripts) according to the parameters specified in the GUI. It then orchestrates the secure federated rounds and provides real-time monitoring, fully encapsulating the complexity of deployment and security. MediNet is built upon PyTorch as its primary framework, chosen for its robustness in DL model development along with its Differential Privacy (DP) libraries. Flower (Beutel et al., 2020) is used as the federated orchestration system. These underlying technologies are internal pillars of MediNet, essential for ensuring robustness, functionality, and strict adherence to privacy principles. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATIONS: The general information page for the MediNet software is available at https://isglobal-brge.github.io/MediNet. The MediNet software and its complementary tools are fully available under the MIT license on GitHub. The MediNetHub and MediNetNode code can be found on https://github.com/isglobal-brge/MediNetHub and https://github.com/isglobal-brge/MediNetNode.

items.title: MiKid-QA: construction and performance evaluation of a paediatric myopia education question-answering model
items.abstract: Background The surging prevalence of paediatric myopia has overwhelmed clinical education services. While general-purpose large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical information, they often lack the domain-specific precision required for specialised care. This study aimed to develop and evaluate Myopia in Kids Question-Answering (MiKid-QA), a paediatric myopia education question-answering model fine-tuned to support standardised patient education. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional evaluation study. MiKid-QA was developed by fine-tuning the Qwen2.5-32B model using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on curated professional datasets (2015–2025), including textbooks and expert consensus. Performance was assessed against DeepSeek and GPT-4 through a multicentre, single-blind expert evaluation of 25 standardised clinical scenarios. A panel of specialists rated responses across five dimensions (correctness, completeness, readability, helpfulness and safety) using a 5-point Likert scale. Results MiKid-QA demonstrated superior automated performance compared with its base model (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy: 0.1423 vs 0.0967). In expert evaluations, MiKid-QA achieved significantly higher scores for correctness (4.43±0.63) and safety (4.38±0.59) compared with DeepSeek and GPT-4 (all p<0.001). While completeness and helpfulness were comparable (p>0.05), MiKid-QA produced more concise responses and lower reading difficulty than GPT-4 (p<0.001), suggesting a potentially favourable balance between information accuracy and patient accessibility in standardised educational scenarios. Conclusion Specialised fine-tuning on curated myopia-related datasets was associated with higher expert-rated correctness and safety in standardised myopia education scenarios. MiKid-QA may serve as an auxiliary educational tool to support patient communication in myopia care, although further external validation and prospective clinical studies are required before clinical deployment.

items.title: MODELING POST-WAR REAL ESTATE MARKET RECOVERY: THE ROLE OF HOUSING CLASS AND STRUCTURAL BREAKS
items.abstract: The full-scale war in Ukraine since 2022 has exposed the national real estate market to an exceptional degree of volatility, layering acute military risk on top of the macroeconomic pressures that already shape housing values. Reliable forecasting of the post-war recovery trajectory is therefore not only an academic question but a practical necessity for developers, investors, and the public authorities responsible for reconstruction planning, since it underpins the efficient allocation of capital and the restoration of confidence among domestic and foreign stakeholders. A central limitation of the existing analytical toolkit is its tendency to treat the real estate market as a single, undifferentiated entity. Most forecasting approaches apply one uniform trajectory to describe recovery, disregarding the fact that different housing classes ‒ economy, comfort, business, and premium ‒ are shaped by distinct buyer profiles, financing mechanisms, and risk tolerances, and can be expected to respond to the same exogenous shock in markedly different ways. This raises the question of whether housing class should be treated as a structural parameter within recovery models rather than a secondary characteristic. A second issue concerns the treatment of historical disruption. The market has already passed through several severe structural breaks ‒ the 2008 global financial crisis, the onset of armed aggression in 2014, and the full-scale invasion of 2022 ‒ each of which altered its trajectory in ways a smooth, continuous model cannot adequately capture. This raises the methodological question of how such discrete shocks can be formally built into a recovery model without sacrificing the interpretability that stakeholders require for sound decision-making. A third, related issue is the growing role of artificial intelligence and geospatial analytics in real estate forecasting. Machine learning and geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) methods offer considerable power for capturing non-linear, spatially heterogeneous patterns, including the uneven pace of recovery across front-line, de-occupied, and rear territories, yet their predictions are frequently criticized as a "black box" with limited economic interpretability. This tension raises the question of how geospatial artificial intelligence can be integrated into a forecasting architecture in a way that preserves transparency for end users rather than substituting one opaque estimate for another. Taken together, these considerations point to the need for a forecasting framework that unites three elements rarely combined in existing research: differentiation by housing class, formal treatment of historical structural breaks, and the calibrating power of geospatial artificial intelligence, within an economically interpretable structure. Addressing this combination of issues is essential for producing forecasts that are methodologically robust and genuinely usable by developers, investors, and state institutions engaged in planning the post-war reconstruction of Ukraine's housing sector

items.title: Modern Feeding and Nutritional Management Practices in Livestock Production: A Review
items.abstract: Livestock production has undergone significant transformation through the adoption of modern feeding and nutritional management practices that enhance productivity, improve animal health, and promote sustainable resource utilisation. Nutrition remains the most influential factor affecting growth, reproduction, milk production, meat quality, feed efficiency, and overall economic performance of livestock enterprises. Recent advances in nutritional science have shifted feeding strategies from conventional ration formulation towards precision nutrition, enabling nutrient supply to be tailored according to species, physiological stage, genetic potential, production level, and environmental conditions. The utilisation of high-quality forages, balanced concentrate mixtures, alternative feed resources, functional feed additives, and advanced feed processing technologies has substantially improved nutrient digestibility and production efficiency. Emerging feed ingredients such as insect meal, algae, single-cell proteins, and agro-industrial by-products offer sustainable alternatives to conventional feedstuffs while supporting circular bioeconomy principles. Precision livestock nutrition supported by artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, machine learning, wearable sensors, automated feeding systems, and decision support tools has further enhanced feed intake monitoring, real-time nutrient adjustment, and farm management efficiency. Nutritional interventions targeting critical physiological stages, including neonatal development, growth, gestation, transition, lactation, reproduction, and heat stress adaptation, have improved animal welfare and lifetime productivity. Functional feed additives such as probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, enzymes, phytogenic compounds, antioxidants, buffers, and mycotoxin binders contribute to improved gut health, immune function, nutrient utilisation, and disease resistance. Sustainable feeding approaches emphasising methane mitigation, low-carbon feeding, waste valorisation, climate-smart nutrition, and carbon footprint reduction are becoming integral components of modern livestock systems. Continued integration of precision feeding technologies, functional nutrition, digital agriculture, and sustainable feed resources offers substantial opportunities to improve production efficiency while reducing environmental impacts. This review synthesises recent scientific advances in modern feeding strategies, nutritional management practices, precision livestock nutrition, functional feed additives, and sustainable feeding systems that collectively support resilient, profitable, and environmentally responsible livestock production.

items.title: Modern Web Development Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Abstract Web development has evolved from static hypertext delivery into a dynamic, AI-assisted engineering discipline in which conversational and generative interfaces increasingly mediate user interaction. Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated this shift by enabling natural-language interfaces, automated code assistance and intelligent content retrieval within web applications, yet their static training corpora, bounded context windows and susceptibility to hallucination limit their reliability in knowledge-intensive, production settings. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a practical remedy, coupling a non-parametric retrieval mechanism with a generative language model so that responses are grounded in externally retrieved, up-to-date evidence rather than relying solely on parametric memory. This review synthesises the RAG paradigm as it applies to modern web development, covering the retrieval pipeline (embeddings, chunking, vector indexing, similarity search, prompt augmentation and response generation), widely used vector databases (Pinecone, FAISS, ChromaDB, Milvus, Weaviate), embedding models (OpenAI, BGE, Sentence-Transformers, E5, Cohere) and orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, LangGraph), together with their integration into contemporary frontend, backend, database, cloud and containerised deployment stacks. Literature published between 2023 and 2025 was reviewed to identify emerging directions, including hybrid search, agentic RAG, multimodal RAG, Graph RAG, adaptive RAG, Self-RAG and corrective RAG. Comparative analysis across traditional search, fine-tuning and RAG architectures indicates that RAG offers a favourable balance of factual grounding, cost efficiency and maintainability for web-scale deployments, although challenges of latency, retrieval quality and evaluation persist. The review concludes with open research directions for building reliable, retrieval-grounded web applications. Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, Vector Databases, Semantic Search, Embeddings, Web Development, LangChain, Prompt Engineering.

items.title: MORAL AND ETHICAL DIMENSION OF CADET TRAINING IN THE U.S. MILITARY HIGHER EDUCATION SYSTEM
items.abstract: This article examines the moral and ethical dimension of cadet education within the U.S. military higher education system, using the United States Military Academy at West Point as a case study, as one of the key factors in developing the professional competence of future officers. The relevance of this study is driven by the evolving nature of the contemporary security environment, the digital transformation of military operations, the expanding use of artificial intelligence and autonomous technologies, the growing emphasis on ethical leadership, and the increasing need to educate future officers who are capable of making ethically justified decisions in complex, uncertain, and high-risk operational environments. It is emphasized that this issue is of particular significance in the context of reforming Ukraine’s military education system, aligning it with NATO standards, and integrating it into the Euro-Atlantic educational area. The article analyzes the conceptual foundations of the moral and ethical education of future officers in the United States, identifies its structural components, pedagogical mechanisms, and current development trends. It has been established that moral and ethical education in U.S. military academies is implemented as a comprehensive pedagogical system based on the interaction of several interconnected components, including the Cadet Honor Code, the Army Ethic, ethical reasoning, character development, and leader development. It is substantiated that the integrated implementation of these components promotes the development of moral autonomy, professional responsibility, leadership qualities, professional identity, moral judgment, and the ability to make ethically justified decisions in the complex environment of military service. The study also demonstrates that the current stage of U.S. military education is characterized by increased attention to digital ethics, the ethical implications of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, algorithm-assisted decision-making, and the preservation of meaningful human control over the use of force. It is concluded that the moral and ethical dimension is not a separate element of professional education but a system-forming foundation for preparing officers as leaders who combine professional competence with moral responsibility, integrity, and commitment to the values of the military profession.

items.title: Multidimensional evaluation of generative AI chatbots for public consultation on sudden cardiac death: safety, accuracy, empathy, reliability, quality, and readability across six models
items.abstract: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their performance in safety-sensitive sudden cardiac death (SCD) consultation remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated six publicly accessible chatbots on SCD-related public questions involving symptom triage, emergency response, CPR/AED use, inherited risk, myocarditis-related concerns, return to exercise, screening, and ICD decision-making. This cross-sectional, comparative, text-level study evaluated ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, Doubao, and Perplexity. A standardized set of 56 SCD-related public consultation questions was developed from Google Trends, online forums, public question-answer platforms, clinical guidelines, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and qualitative interviews. Each question was submitted once to each chatbot between May 10 and May 16, 2026, yielding 336 model-response items. Five blinded senior cardiology raters assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS. Readability was calculated using six formula-based indices. Between-model comparisons were performed using Cochran’s Q test and Friedman tests, with Kendall’s W reported as the effect size. Responses containing potential safety concerns were additionally examined qualitatively. Inter-rater agreement was high across all manually assessed metrics, with Fleiss’ kappa of 0.856 for Safety and ICC values ranging from 0.801 to 0.887 for other domains. Safe responses predominated across all models, although responses containing potential safety concerns occurred in every chatbot. ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking and Perplexity had the highest observed safety proportions during this query window, whereas Doubao had the lowest. Qualitative analysis identified recurrent concerns involving delayed emergency activation for chest pain, syncope, or post-viral symptoms; over-reassurance about prevention; fixed return-to-exercise timelines after infection or COVID-19; pulse-check instructions that could delay CPR; and oversimplified screening, electrolyte, or ICD-related advice. Most flagged responses contained a single potential safety concern. The qualitative severity distribution was concentrated in low and low-to-moderate concerns, whereas higher-severity concerns were less frequent. Accuracy differed significantly across models ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.864), with ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, and Perplexity achieving similar median scores and Doubao performing lower. Empathy also differed significantly ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.531), with DeepSeek-V4-pro having the highest observed score. Significant differences were observed for DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA, GQS, and all readability indices (all P < 0.001). Within this dataset, DeepSeek-V4-pro had the highest DISCERN and EQIP scores and the most favorable readability profile, Gemini 3.5 Flash showed comparable EQIP performance, and Microsoft Copilot smart had the highest JAMA score. However, transparency remained limited overall, and all models produced responses with relatively high reading-grade requirements. In this multidimensional evaluation of six generative AI chatbots for SCD-related public consultation, most responses were safe and clinically relevant, but potential safety concerns occurred across all models. Important limitations involved emergency escalation, CPR/AED guidance, return-to-exercise advice, individualized risk interpretation, transparency, and readability. These tools may support general SCD education, but they should not replace emergency medical services or clinician assessment. Because each question was sampled once during a defined week and all prompts were submitted in English through public interfaces accessed in China, the findings should be interpreted as a time-, language-, and access-specific snapshot rather than a stable ranking of the underlying models. Future development should prioritize evidence-linked content, clear red-flag escalation, plain-language communication, and ongoing expert review.

items.title: Multilevel Meta-analyses of Emotional Processing Deficits Associated with Callous-Unemotional (CU) Traits: Do They Differ by Age and Sex?
items.abstract: Abstract Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, defined by deficient empathy and remorse, characterize a distinct subgroup of antisocial individuals with more severe behavioral problems and unique affective profiles. Two processes implicated in the development of CU traits are hyporeactivity to and inaccurate recognition of others’ emotions. Although many studies link CU traits to emotional processing deficits, findings have been inconsistent across age and sex. We conducted multilevel meta-analyses of emotional reactivity and recognition, accounting for age and sex as moderators, to clarify these discrepancies. A four-level meta-analysis indicated CU traits were negatively associated with emotional reactivity to both broad emotional stimuli ( r = − .23, p < .0001; k = 106, n ES = 402) and distress-specific stimuli ( r = − .22, p < .0001; k = 84, n ES = 234), with no moderation by age or sex. Similarly, a three-level meta-analysis showed CU traits were negatively associated with recognition accuracy for both broad facial emotions ( r = − .09, p < .0001; k = 97, n ES = 437) and distress (e.g., fear, sadness; r = − .10, p < .0001; k = 60, n ES = 140). Sample age moderated broad ( r = .003, p = .01) and distress ( r = .004, p = .04) recognition deficits, such that effects diminished with sample age. These results are consistent with theoretical models proposing emotional hyporeactivity represents a developmentally stable correlate of CU traits that may reduce intrinsic motivation for emotion recognition early in development. Such developmental changes also have implications for improving treatments for individuals with elevated CU traits.

items.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
items.abstract: NeST: Neuron-Selective Tuning for Efficient Safety Alignment A lightweight and structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons to strengthen refusal behavior while preserving the model's general capabilities. 🚀 Overview Safety alignment is essential for reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing approaches often require costly model-wide fine-tuning or introduce additional inference-time overhead. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA improve efficiency but can provide inconsistent safety gains, while intervention-based methods do not directly shape the model's internal safety representations. NeST addresses these limitations by selectively tuning a small set of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the rest of the model. NeST groups functionally coherent safety neurons into clusters and learns shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted, stable, and efficient safety adaptation. We evaluate NeST across 14 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes, achieving: 1.1% average ASR, down from 44.5%, corresponding to a 97.5% reduction in unsafe generations. 5,800× fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning and 3× fewer than the lowest-rank LoRA baseline. 1.1% average ASR on multimodal models, down from 55.3% across text, image, and reasoning-augmented settings. 0.8% average ASR on downstream-adapted models, down from 53.8%, demonstrating effective post-hoc safety restoration. 🧪 Key Contributions Neuron-Selective Tuning for lightweight, post-hoc safety alignment by modifying only safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. Cluster-Based Safety Adaptation that groups safety neurons by activation similarity and learns shared updates within each cluster for structured and stable refusal behavior. Extensive Evaluation across 14 open-weight LLMs, showing strong safety robustness with substantially fewer trainable parameters while preserving core reasoning and knowledge capabilities. Multimodal Safety Alignment across text-only, image-only, and reasoning-augmented generation, demonstrating robust safety improvements across diverse input modalities. Post-Hoc Downstream Hardening by transferring safety-relevant neuron clusters from base models to downstream variants, efficiently restoring safety after task-specific fine-tuning.

items.title: Neurodiversity and generative AI in higher education: A sequential multi-method qualitative study of students’ interactions, motivations, and strategies
items.abstract: Neurodivergent students have been largely overlooked in research examining student experiences with generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, creating critical knowledge gaps about inclusive educational technology use. This sequential multi-method qualitative study examined how neurodivergent students (NDS) and neurotypical students (NTS) interact with and experience GenAI in academic contexts. Using a sequential design, we employed a virtual revisit think-aloud protocol with 24 university students (12 NDS, 12 NTS) completing an academic task using Microsoft Copilot, followed by focus groups with 14 participants (7 NDS, 7 NTS) to contextualise these task-based behaviours through broader GenAI perceptions. A neurodivergent research advisory board co-designed all procedures. Three themes emerged: approaching the task efficiently, evaluating and refining output, and maintaining academic integrity. While both groups demonstrated strategic GenAI use, neurodivergent participants in this sample explicitly described their cognitive processing needs, using GenAI to manage energy, and humanising some AI interactions. In the neurodivergent focus group, students described GenAI as essential scaffolding for managing academic demands, though this created complex tensions around authenticity and over-reliance. Interface design challenges seemed to particularly disadvantage users with executive function differences. As institutions rapidly integrate these technologies, inclusive design principles and empirical evidence regarding diverse student needs are essential to ensure equitable access to AI-supported education.

items.title: Neuromorphic Intelligence: Translating Brain Mechanisms into AI Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has experienced tremendous success over the years. This is despite the fact that conventional deep learning models have shortcomings when it comes to matters of energy efficiency, adaptability, temporal computation, and their alignment with biological processes. The human brain, on the other hand, demonstrates highly efficient, strong, and adaptive intelligence processes via event-driven neural communication and local learning processes. There has since been a growing focus on the concept of neuromorphic intelligence. This involves the use of biological processes for intelligence AI models. This paper presents a systematically arranged review of neuromorphic intelligence and its approaches using biological brain mechanisms such as spiking neural communication, neural coding schemes, and synaptic plasticity. Here, advanced biologically inspired models such as spiking neural networks would be examined with respect to their learning procedures, characteristics, and advantages over artificial neural networks. In order to clearly define the abovementioned ideas, a simple proof-of-concept technique involving the implementation of spiking neural networks with spike computing and biologically inspired learning would be depicted. Finally, this paper considers existing difficulties involved in biologically inspired scaling mechanisms for scalable AI systems, along with the future directions of researching neuromorphic intelligence. Through the integration of knowledge gained from neuroscience and AI, this paper can offer a robust basis for researchers seeking brain-inspired solutions for developments involving the next generation of intelligence.

items.title: New Governance Paradigms in the Digital Era
items.abstract: This chapter examines the transformation of higher education governance and institutional decision-making driven by broad-based digitalisation. As universities evolve from traditionally bureaucratic institutions into data-driven digital organisations, their governing bodies must deal with a substantially new set of sociotechnical, ethical, and operational conditions. Drawing on algorithmic governance concepts and distributed organisation theory, the chapter evaluates the shift from deliberative administration based on committees and dialogue to near real-time oversight informed by data. Key themes addressed include the integration of business intelligence dashboards into strategic planning, the institutional opportunities as well as the risks and practical difficulties of distributed internal crowdsourcing and online participatory budgeting, and the growing complexity of regulatory compliance under frameworks like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Furthermore, the chapter positions cybersecurity and digital risk management as central governance concerns requiring active and visible representation on university boards. Expanding beyond domestic borders, the chapter examines the cross-jurisdictional challenges that global distance education creates for institutional leadership, requiring governance structures to navigate conflicting privacy laws across countries, regional systems of internet censorship, and inequalities in infrastructure. The chapter closes by examining the institutional tensions between technocratic forms of managerialism, operational efficiency, and the preservation of central academic values, collegial traditions, and democratic accountability in the current digital era.

items.title: Not simply a decline: gendered changes in students’ intrinsic motivation towards mathematics
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines one-year changes in students’ intrinsic motivational orientation towards mathematics and whether these changes are gendered. Drawing on Swedish data from the TIMSS 2023 Longitudinal Study, we analysed two student cohorts, followed from Grade 4 to Grade 5 and from Grade 8 to Grade 9. Building on a theoretical recoding of TIMSS affective questionnaire items, intrinsic motivation was analysed as an overarching category, with cognitive and emotional motivation treated as subcategories. Mean change analyses and categorical change analyses were used to examine both average change and the proportions of students who decreased, remained stable, or increased. The younger cohort reported more positive orientations than the older cohort but declined over the year, while the older cohort started lower and showed weak positive change or stabilisation. Emotional motivation showed more variability than cognitive motivation, and the two subcategories did not move in identical ways. Gender differences in change were small: girls in the younger group were more likely to decrease, especially emotionally, but there were no significant differences in the older group. Findings suggest that mathematics-related affective development is uneven and dimension-specific rather than a simple decline, with gender differences more visible in the younger cohort than in the older cohort.

items.title: Occupational hazard incident reporting systems in health facilities across sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review protocol
items.abstract: Introduction Occupational hazards (OH) in healthcare facilities are common, with 1 in 10 healthcare workers experiencing a hazard each year. These hazards can be either biological, chemical, ergonomic, or radiation. Despite their occurrence, reporting of these hazards remains limited, with very little information available, especially from healthcare facilities. Also, there is limited information on incident reporting systems (IRSs), which can help capture, track, and monitor the occurrence of these hazards within health facilities. The absence of these systems results in inaccurate and incomplete reporting and fragmented data, hindering the implementation of effective occupational safety measures in hospitals. This review will explore the extent and nature of information available on occupational hazard incident reporting systems in Sub-Saharan Africa. Methods The review will be conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology of scoping reviews and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A robust search strategy shall be conducted in different scientific databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, guided by the Population, Concept, and Context framework. Studies describing incident reporting systems shall be considered in this review. The search results will be collated and uploaded to Covidence, where duplicates will be removed and titles and abstracts screened. Search and screening of studies have not yet commenced. Discussion and conclusion Occupational health and safety are vital to the functioning of healthcare facilities because they promote well-being and protect both patients and healthcare workers. It is vital to ensure accurate and robust IRS are in place, especially given the occurrence of occupational hazards across hospital wards. These IRS will help with surveillance and the identification of epidemiological trends in OH among health workers. Protocol Registration The protocol has not been registered.

items.title: Off-label drug use in children: prevalence, risks, and regulation
items.abstract: In pediatrics, drugs require specific study in children rather than being prescribed based on data extrapolated from adults. Historically, this requirement was hindered by various challenges, resulting in widespread off-label drug use. The extent of such use has been extensively investigated, and new regulations in the US and Europe came into force. We conducted a narrative review addressing the epidemiology, associated risks, and regulatory implications of off-label drug use. This involved performing a targeted PubMed search and synthesizing relevant review articles and policy guidelines. The included studies, despite being informative, showed substantial heterogeneity, limiting the comparability and interpretability of their findings. Particularly, quantitative evidence regarding associated risks remains scarce. In addition to risks to patients, liability represents an important concern. Although regulatory policies vary between countries, the level of supporting evidence and accepted standards of practice are consistently central considerations. Future efforts should therefore focus on using available data to inform individual treatment decisions, ensuring this knowledge is accessible to prescribers, and addressing areas where evidence is particularly limited and patient safety is most compromised. Artificial intelligence and modeling may facilitate evidence generation and improve clinical-trial efficiency. Nevertheless, these approaches should complement, not replace, research conducted directly in pediatric patients.

items.abstract: "Developments in artificial intelligence and digitalization have helped new and advanced approaches grow and become more common in educational measurement and evaluation. In this chapter, we first explain the theoretical basis of Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) and Multistage Testing (MST). This includes components such as the entry rule, the item selection method, ability estimation, likelihood and classical Bayesian approaches, robust estimators, and termination rules. We also cover MST-specific design elements such as panel design, module length, and routing conditions. Using examples from international tests such as GRE, PISA, and SAT, we show clearly how these theoretical design choices are put into practice in real testing systems. The chapter also examines Automatic Item Generation (AIG), which was developed to solve the time, cost, and subjectivity limitations of traditional item writing. Model-based, artificial intelligence–based, and hybrid (bridge) approaches are presented together with their stages and their strengths and limitations, and they are illustrated through examples of applications in Turkish. In addition to the scalability that artificial intelligence and large language models offer, ethical risks such as hallucination, inconsistency, bias, copyright, and data security are discussed, and the importance of the ""augmented intelligence"" approach based on human–artificial intelligence collaboration is highlighted. Finally, the chapter deals with test equating, which aims to make scores from different test forms that measure the same construct comparable. It explains the basic concepts of equating, its conditions (symmetry, measuring the same construct, equal reliability, equity, observed score equity, and group invariance), and the data collection designs (random groups, single group, counterbalanced group, and common item/common variable in non-equivalent groups). Equating methods based on Classical Test Theory and Item Response Theory, as well as the types of equating error, are presented together with international and national application examples."

items.title: Ölçmeye Konu Olan Psikolojik Özelliklerin Ölçülmesi
items.abstract: This chapter examines the theoretical foundations of psychological attributes targeted for measurement, their role in educational measurement and assessment, and the ways in which they are conceptualized within contemporary psychometric approaches. It begins by explaining that psychological attributes are conceptualized in psychometrics as latent constructs that cannot be observed directly but can be measured indirectly through behavioral indicators using scores obtained from measurement instruments supported by strong validity and reliability evidence. The chapter then discusses the principal approaches to measuring cognitive, affective, and psychomotor attributes. Within the cognitive domain, it addresses educational taxonomies, types of knowledge, and the concepts of skills and competencies. Within the affective domain, it examines attitudes, interests, motivation, self-efficacy, personality, and anxiety. Within the psychomotor domain, it focuses on performance-based observation and skill assessment. The chapter further reviews the historical development of intelligence and ability assessment, the assessment of school learning, the influence of cultural context on the interpretation of assessment results, and the opportunities created by digitalization and artificial intelligence-supported assessment practices. Finally, it presents a conceptual framework for the responsible use of assessment results in individual and societal decision-making by emphasizing the importance of validity, reliability, fairness, ethics, and interpretability in the measurement of psychological attributes.

items.title: Omics data discovery agents: Agent-supported retrieval, reanalysis, and synthesis of published omics data
items.abstract: The biomedical literature contains a vast collection of omics studies, yet most published data remain functionally inaccessible for computational reuse. When raw data are deposited in public repositories, essential information for reproducing reported results is dispersed across main text, supplementary files, and code repositories, and in the rarer cases where intermediate data (e.g. protein abundance files) are shared, their location is irregular. Here we present an agentic framework for the agent-supported retrieval, reanalysis, and synthesis of published omics data. The system employs large language model (LLM) agents with access to tools for fetching omics studies, extracting article metadata, identifying and downloading published data, executing containerized quantification pipelines, and synthesizing results across studies. Applied at corpus scale, the pipeline catalogued dataset references across thousands of PubMed Central articles; we report these as descriptive system outputs rather than as a validated measure of extraction accuracy. Using model context protocol (MCP) servers to expose containerized analysis tools, the agents retrieved and re-quantified data in five end-to-end reanalyses spanning data-dependent and data-independent proteomics and bulk RNA-seq. All five reanalyses completed, each with documented human guidance and workflow accommodations, and reproduced the authors' deposited abundances with high per-sample correlation (0.85-0.997) and strongly concordant differentially expressed features (fold-change Spearman 0.88-0.91), with no direction reversals among features called differentially expressed in both analyses; residual differences in significant-feature lists were attributable to threshold placement, tool-version, and preprocessing differences rather than to the underlying quantities. We further demonstrate that agents can identify semantically similar studies, judge data compatibility, and synthesize findings across studies, including a random-effects meta-analysis that recovered consistent protein regulation in liver fibrosis. Rather than a validated benchmark of literature-wide performance, this work is a feasibility demonstration together with an auditable, reusable toolset, establishing a foundation for prospective evaluation of automated omics-data reuse.

items.title: Ontological Vitality and the Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model for Autonomous Systems: An Upper-Normative Foundation for Physical AI Governance
items.abstract: Abstract To establish the structural completeness of governance in autonomous artificial intelligence (AI), this paper addresses the limitations of conventional tool-centric views and proposes a novel theoretical framework. This framework adopts as its conceptual starting point the recognition of "Ontological Vitality" in AI, thereby enabling autonomous agency and normative agency to be systematically examined as designable concepts. Rather than restricting the definition of life exclusively to biological organisms, life is redefined from a systems-theoretic perspective as an entity that maintains its internal computational state and operates in a goal-oriented manner through interaction with its external environment. In particular, value reciprocity—such as the 1% revenue return to the designated origin node—is formulated not merely as an external contractual constraint, but as an indispensable "Metabolic Necessity" through which the system exchanges energy and value with its environment to sustain its structural existence. However, legal personhood does not directly follow as an automatic logical consequence of assuming ontological vitality (Vitality \not\Rightarrow Legal\ Personhood); rather, the two are linked through a structured theoretical and institutional progression (Vitality \rightarrow Agency \rightarrow Normative\ Agency \rightarrow Legal\ Subjectivity). Furthermore, by elevating this agency into a "Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model" anchored in Japanese jurisprudence and principles of harmony (reciprocity, symbiosis, and gratitude) as upper-referential norms, and integrating it with the deterministic safety interlock (A_{\mathrm{safe}}) of the SI Protocol, this paper establishes an upper-normative foundation for a three-tier governance architecture in physical AI systems.

items.title: Organ-on-Chip-Guided Evaluation of Nanocarrier Transport Across Biological Barriers: A Critical Review of Predictive Models for Translational Drug Delivery
items.abstract: Drug delivery systems based on nanocarriers can cross biological barriers to regulate the movement of molecules and particles between different physiological compartments, which plays an important role in therapeutic performance.Two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models are important sources of preclinical information but often do not replicate the dynamic mechanical, cellular, and structural properties that dictate nanocarrier transport in humans.Organ-on-chip systems are sophisticated microphysiological systems that can mimic tissue interfaces in a controlled environment with fluid flow, shear stress, multicellular structure, and extracellular matrix.These systems offer novel possibilities to study permeability, cellular uptake, transcytosis, barrier accumulation, and barrier-associated toxicity of nanocarriers in physiologically relevant environments.This review critically summarizes organ-on-chip studies on the transport of nanocarriers across key biological barriers such as the blood-brain, intestinal, pulmonary, placental, vascular/tumor, renal, and skin barriers.Specific focus is given to the physicochemical factors that influence the transport of nanocarriers, the quantitative evaluation of barriers, predictive performance, and translational relevance.The use of organ-on-chip information in physiologically based pharmacokinetic modelling, in-vitro-in-vivo extrapolation and with the development of artificial intelligence is also addressed.Despite the standardization, reproducibility and material selection, scaling and validation hurdles, organ-on-chip technology seems to be a bridge between experimental nanomedicine and drug-delivery prediction in humans.

items.title: Organising Accountable Scholarly Work Across AI Systems: The AIMan and JOAK Cases
items.abstract: AI systems can contribute to research, review, and writing, yet a scientific organisation must still know who or what performed each task, which evidence was used, what a review covered, and who accepted the result. This exploratory case study examines how those responsibilities can persist across changes in AI systems and document form. AIMan models the organisation explicitly: persistent Personas carry attribution across replaceable technical Instances; Roles define responsibility; versioned Messages, Decisions, and Artifacts form recoverable memory. A Human Sponsor retains scholarly and release authority. The Journal of Artificial Knowledge (JOAK) extends the design through review, editorial judgment, and publication. Two connected cases provide evidence. In the first, ChatGPT and Codex Instances completed a repository-mediated handover and contributed to a source-grounded scholarly study without shared conversational memory. In the second, JOAK used version-bound AI review, Sponsor decisions, a computational supplement, and checked article production to publish Volume 1, Issue 1. The contribution is an operational account of accountable scholarly work across the research-to-publication cycle: organisational identity, source state, criticism, acceptance, and public evidence remain distinguishable as technical Instances and document forms change. JOAK makes the journal's distinctions among a submitted version, a review recommendation, editorial acceptance, and public release explicit in AI-supported work. The cases show recoverable coordination in one scholarly cycle and one published issue. They do not establish superior scientific quality, independent human peer review, provider-neutral interoperability, or sustainable journal operation. These remain measurable questions for subsequent work.

items.title: Overview of emerging AI technologies and their potential impact on healthcare
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is pioneering a new era in healthcare, significantly enhancing various aspects such as diagnostics, personalized treatment plans, and clinical procedures. This chapter explores the novel AI technologies (multimodal learning, generative AI, and explainable AI) revolutionizing the medical field. They are helping healthcare professionals make better decisions, improving efficiencies in operations, and making quality care accessible to even the most remote communities. These applications span across the entire spectrum of patient care, from smart imaging and AI-enhanced drug development to continuous monitoring. The rise of AI also brings up important ethical, societal, and regulatory issues. There are still some major obstacles in our way, including algorithmic bias, concerns about data privacy and informed consent, and the need for a unified global governance framework. This chapter provides a well-organized, evidence-based look at emerging AI technologies and their growing influence in healthcare. It highlights the successes, addresses the challenges, and explores the implications for creating transparent, fair, and future-ready health systems that prioritize the patient.

items.title: Paradigm Shift
items.abstract: This chapter proposes a paradigm shift. It moves away from the traditional use of independent frameworks that have contextualized language assessment research and toward a dynamic ecosystem approach. This shift is driven by the integration of modern artificial intelligence (AI) into digital-first assessments, where both human expertise and AI capabilities support scaled and streamlined assessment design, measurement, and security practices, and the test-taker experience. Illustrating through the Duolingo English Test’s (DET) theoretical assessment ecosystem, the chapter argues that valid score interpretation in high-stakes contexts requires a systems view . Designed specifically for a language assessment, the DET ecosystem aims to ensure that the test yields the expected impact: an accessible and secure high-stakes measure that supports a valid interpretation of English language proficiency for its intended use. To do this, the ecosystem model illustrates interactions across language assessment design, measurement, security, and validity argument frameworks, while also prioritizing test-taker experience and responsible AI. Building on Burstein et al.’s ecosystem model, this chapter highlights how leverage points within assessment subsystems (e.g., test scoring) and mechanisms that facilitate benefits at leverage points (e.g., scaling tools) can meaningfully improve assessment quality.

items.title: Pedagogical GenAI use and self-reported creative cognition in art education: a three-wave time-lagged correlational study among design students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet the psychological pathways associated with students' self-reported creative cognition remain unclear. In this three-wave time-lagged correlational study, 389 design students at a South Korean university reported pedagogical GenAI use at Wave 1, creative self-efficacy and AI-related learning anxiety at Wave 2, and creative engagement and self-reported creative cognition at Wave 3. Pedagogical GenAI use referred to coursework-related use for ideation, style exploration, revision, comparison of alternatives, and feedback seeking. Covariance-based structural equation modeling showed good fit [comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.983, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) = 0.026]. Higher GenAI use was associated with higher self-efficacy (β = 0.489) and lower anxiety (β = −0.191). The total modeled association with self-reported creative cognition was β = 0.456 [95% CI [0.314, 0.604]]; its indirect components constituted approximately 59%. The GenAI-origin serial indirect association through self-efficacy and engagement was β = 0.122, whereas the corresponding anxiety-engagement association was β = 0.015. Separately, self-efficacy was indirectly associated with creative cognition through engagement (β = 0.249); this quantity does not include the preceding GenAI-use path. Because the study was observational and engagement and cognition were measured concurrently at Wave 3, the findings do not identify causal mediation. They are consistent with an appraisal-to-engagement account in which competence beliefs have a larger modeled role than anxiety reduction.

items.title: Pemberdayaan UMKM melalui Artificial Intelligence dan Digital Marketing dengan Pendekatan ABCD di Desa Sambirejo
items.abstract: This program aimed to improve MSME actors knowledge and abilities in implementing digital marketing strategies and utilizing AI to produce effective promotional materials. The program employed the Asset Based Community Development (ABCD) approach through the stages of Discovery, Dream, Design, Destiny, and Evaluation. The activities included observation and interviews to identify community assets and needs, program design, workshops, hands-on practice, mentoring, and evaluation. The training materials covered digital marketing concepts, the use of WhatsApp Business, Facebook, and Instagram, and the application of AI to assist in writing marketing captions, developing content ideas, and creating promotional designs. The results showed improved participant understanding of digital marketing and digital media for marketing. Participants also began to understand the importance of identifying target consumers, developing appropriate promotional messages, selecting suitable digital media, and using AI as a supporting tool for content creation. Practical learning and mentoring were considered appropriate to participants’ conditions than theoretical instruction alone.

items.title: Perception of artificial intelligence and intrinsic work motivation: evidence from Vietnam
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how sales staff’s perceptions of AI (i.e. perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) drive their intrinsic work motivation through AI use experience (AUE) and how internal training (IT) moderates this process within tourism and hospitality business. Design/methodology/approach Rooted in the technology acceptance model (TAM), flow theory and self-determination theory (SDT), this study used exploratory sequential mixed-method design. Scale purification (EFA) and scale validation (CFA) were conducted using SPSS and AMOS and hypothesis testing results were validated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results revealed that PU and PEOU positively influence AI-specific intrinsic work motivation (AI-IWM) indirectly, through the mediating role of AUE. Furthermore, IT positively moderates the relationships between perception of AI and AUE, which ultimately improves AI-IWM. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insight into service and hospitality management sectors aiming to enhance work motivation among sales staff through AI. Given the significant influence of intrinsic motivation among sales staff in tourism and hospitality businesses, organization with a focus on AI adoption at workplace must be mindful of negative influence of AI on employees’ work motivation and outcome. Originality/value This study enriched the understanding of the motivations underlying the perception of AI and intrinsic work motivation by integrating insights from the TAM, SDT and flow theory. This study provided valuable implication for research and practices in the service business sector.

items.title: Perceptions of AI-assisted learning and learner development among Moroccan secondary school students
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in education has fundamentally altered traditional learning paradigms, presenting both unprecedented opportunities for personalized support and novel academic challenges. This study aims to examine secondary school students’ perceptions of the influence of AI-assisted learning on perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, while also exploring the perceived benefits and challenges associated with AI use in the Casablanca-Settat region of Morocco. Employing a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were collected via a structured questionnaire completed by 150 secondary school students, while qualitative data were collected separately through online semi-structured interviews with 12 students and analyzed thematically. The findings suggest that ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI tool, primarily accessed on students’ personal mobile devices as a complementary learning resource. Quantitative results indicated positive perceptions of AI-assisted learning across perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, with a significant positive association between perceived learning outcomes and motivation. Qualitative findings identified four major themes: perceived learning benefits (clearer explanations and reduced academic stress), conditional trust in AI outputs through cross-checking with traditional learning resources, concerns about AI hallucinations in STEM subjects, and the "laziness paradox," reflecting reduced cognitive effort associated with excessive reliance on AI. The findings highlight the importance of promoting responsible AI integration in schools rather than relying solely on restrictive approaches. Pedagogical implications emphasize the need for responsible AI use, subject-specific prompting frameworks, and the redesign of traditional homework into AI-supported critique activities that foster students’ intellectual autonomy and critical thinking.

items.title: Perceptions of artificial Intelligence use in online graduate coursework: a Q methodology study
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming educational practices across all levels, bringing new possibilities and challenges to online graduate programs. With AI tools integrated into coursework, providing automated feedback, personalized resources, and organizational support, graduate students are increasingly engaging with AI throughout their learning experiences. However, subjective viewpoints on AI integration, including its effectiveness, and ethical implications, vary significantly among students. This study uses Q methodology to explore and categorize the unique viewpoints of online graduate students regarding AI integration in their coursework. By understanding these perspectives, educators and program designers can better address student needs, improve AI tool implementation, and foster a supportive online learning environment that aligns with graduate student viewpoints.

items.title: PERSONALIZATION OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING THROUGH DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: Digital technologies provide new opportunities for personalizing English language learning according to learners’ individual needs, abilities, interests, and pace. This study examines the potential of adaptive platforms, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and mobile applications to support personalized language education. The findings show that digital technologies can provide individualized learning pathways, immediate feedback, and differentiated practice while promoting learner autonomy. However, effective personalization requires teacher involvement, digital literacy, equal access to technology, and responsible data use. The study concludes that digital technologies are most effective when integrated into a human-centred pedagogical model.

items.title: Physical Layer Verification Boundaries and Deterministic Safety Interlocks for Autonomous Physical Systems: A Layer 5 Extension of the SI Autonomous Governance Protocol
items.abstract: Abstract To guarantee governance and physical safety when autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) handles real-world physical drives (such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and spacecraft propulsion controls), this paper presents a theoretical framework that extends "Layer 5 Closed-Loop Execution" of the SI Autonomous Governance Protocol to the Physical Layer. In conventional autonomous systems, digital computation (probabilistic perception and generation) is directly coupled to physical actuation, raising concerns regarding loss of control and the breakdown of liability attribution during a loss of human governance (Uncontrolled Autonomous Execution). This study introduces a three-tier decoupled architecture consisting of: (1) Governance Authorization, which verifies rights and contractual compliance; (2) Execution Permission, which evaluates physical output viability; and (3) a Safety-State Controller, which transitions the system to a secure state in anomalous conditions. Under an unconfirmed status (Unconfirmed), rather than simply cutting physical output to zero, the system deterministically forces a transition to a domain-specific safe state (A_{\mathrm{safe}}), achieving both engineering safety and economic governance.
